sections.h: James, the Lord's brother, and the letter
sections.b: The letter's writer calls himself only "James, a slave of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ" (James 1:1). Tradition identifies him with James the brother of Jesus, whom Paul met in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19) and counted among the "pillars" (Galatians 2:9), who led the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:13-21) and to whom the risen Jesus appeared (1 Corinthians 15:7). Hegesippus, quoted by Eusebius, says he "has been called the Just by all", and Josephus records that the high priest Ananus had him stoned. That the writer does not mention being Jesus' brother is read either as humility or as a sign that someone else wrote in his name.
sections.refs: James 1:1; Galatians 1:19; Galatians 2:9; Acts 15:13-21; Acts 21:18; 1 Corinthians 15:7; Matthew 13:55

sections.b: James asks whether a faith with no works can save (James 2:14) and answers with the examples of Abraham, "justified by works" when he offered Isaac (James 2:21), and Rahab (James 2:25), concluding: "So you see that it is by works that a person is justified, and not by faith alone" (James 2:24). This is the only verse in the Bible with the words "faith alone". The faith James rejects is belief without obedience ("The demons believe it as well", James 2:19), and the works he demands are deeds of mercy (James 2:15-16). How this fits Paul's "justified by faith, apart from works of the law" (Romans 3:28) is set out on the James 2 chapter page, with each church's answer.

common: James and Paul are usually read as answering different questions: Paul how a sinner is accepted by God, James what kind of faith is real.
uncommon: Luther in 1522 judged James "flatly against St. Paul" on this point and would not count it among the chief books of the New Testament.

sections.b: For James, faith is tested by trials (James 1:3), must ask without doubting (James 1:6), must not be mixed with favoritism (James 2:1), and is dead without works (James 2:17, 26). Belief that God is one is good, but the demons share it (James 2:19). The model is Abraham, whose "faith was at work along with his works" (James 2:22), and the "prayer that comes from faith" saves the sick (James 5:15).

James is the New Testament's wisdom book. Wisdom is God's gift to anyone who asks without doubting (James 1:5-8). It is known by its fruit: the wisdom from above is "clean... peaceable, fair-minded, open to persuasion, full of mercy and good fruits" (James 3:17), while jealousy and rivalry are an earthly, demonic counterfeit (James 3:14-16). Like Proverbs, James treats wisdom as a way of life rather than cleverness.
sections.refs: James 1:5-8; James 3:13-18; Proverbs 2:6; Wisdom of Solomon 7:22-23

sections.b: No book of the New Testament says more about speech. Be "ready to listen, slow to talk" (James 1:19); a religion that does not bridle the tongue is empty (James 1:26). The tongue is a small member like a bit or a rudder, a fire lit from Gehenna, a restless evil no one can tame; with it we bless God and curse people made in his likeness (James 3:1-12). James also forbids slander (James 4:11), grumbling (James 5:9) and oaths (James 5:12).
sections.refs: James 1:19; James 1:26; James 3:1-12; James 4:11; James 5:9; James 5:12; Proverbs 18:21

sections.b: James is the New Testament's sharpest critic of the rich. The rich man will wither like a wildflower (James 1:10-11); the rich drag believers into court and insult the name they bear (James 2:6-7); merchants plan profits without God (James 4:13-16); and landowners who cheated their reapers are told to weep, for their riches have rotted and their gold has rusted (James 5:1-6). The church must not flatter the rich in its meetings (James 2:1-4).

James' readers are mostly poor: unpaid reapers (James 5:4), brothers and sisters without food and clothing (James 2:15), the lowly brother who will be raised (James 1:9). God chose "the poor, poor as the world counts it" to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom (James 2:5). True religion is to visit orphans and widows (James 1:27), and faith that does not feed the hungry is dead (James 2:15-17).
sections.refs: James 1:9; James 1:27; James 2:2-6; James 2:15-17; James 5:4; Luke 6:20

sections.b: James calls Leviticus 19:18 "the royal law": "If you truly carry out the royal law, as the Scripture puts it, 'You are to love your neighbor as yourself,' you do well" (James 2:8). Favoritism toward the rich breaks it (James 2:9), and the whole law stands or falls together (James 2:10-11). Other commands of Leviticus 19 run through the letter: no favoritism (Leviticus 19:15), no slander (Leviticus 19:16), prompt wages (Leviticus 19:13).

James speaks of the law only with praise: "the complete law, the law of freedom" (James 1:25; 2:12), "the royal law" (James 2:8). Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point is answerable for all of it (James 2:10). Readers differ on whether he means the Torah itself, the Torah as Jesus taught it, or the gospel. Luther set James' "law of liberty" against Paul's teaching on the law.

"Is one of you ill? Let him send for the elders of the church" (James 5:14). The elders pray and anoint with oil in the Lord's name, and "the prayer that comes from faith will save the one who is worn down by sickness, and the Lord will raise him up" (James 5:15). James joins healing with forgiveness and mutual confession (James 5:16), and points to Elijah as proof that a righteous person's prayer is powerful (James 5:17-18).

James tells the elders of the church to anoint the sick "with oil in the name of the Lord" (James 5:14). The verb is aleipho, the ordinary word for rubbing on oil, used also of the Twelve anointing the sick in Mark 6:13. From this text come the Catholic sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick (once called extreme unction) and the Orthodox mystery of Holy Unction; the Reformers rejected it as a sacrament, and Pentecostal churches practice anointing with prayer for divine healing. The churches' views are set out on the James 5 chapter page.

James opens and closes with prayer: ask God for wisdom in faith (James 1:5-6), and pray in suffering, sing in joy, pray over the sick, pray for one another (James 5:13-16). Prayer fails when it is double-minded (James 1:6-8) or selfish (James 4:3). Elijah, "a man who felt what we feel", shows that "the request of a righteous person, when it is put to work, is very strong" (James 5:16-18).

James presents Elijah as an ordinary man ("a man who felt what we feel") whose prayer stopped and then brought back the rain (James 5:17-18). James, like Luke 4:25, gives the drought as "three years and six months", where 1 Kings 18:1 has "in the third year". 1 Kings does not mention Elijah praying for the drought, but shows him praying, face between his knees, before the rain (1 Kings 18:42).

James asks: "Take Abraham our father. When he laid his son Isaac on the altar as an offering, was he not justified by works?" (James 2:21). He says the offering of Isaac fulfilled the Scripture "Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness" (James 2:23; Genesis 15:6), and calls Abraham "the friend of God" (James 2:23; 2 Chronicles 20:7). Paul reads the same verse to show Abraham was counted righteous before he did anything (Romans 4:2-10).

sections.h: The binding of Isaac in James
sections.b: James makes the binding of Isaac the moment Abraham was "justified by works" and his faith "made complete" (James 2:21-22), following the Jewish tradition that counted it Abraham's great test: "Abraham: was he not found faithful in the test, and was it not reckoned to him as righteousness?" (1 Maccabees 2:52).

James pairs Rahab with Abraham: "Rahab the prostitute was the same. She took in the messengers and sent them away by a different road. Was she not justified by works?" (James 2:25). Hebrews 11:31 praises the same act as faith. The patriarch and the Canaanite outsider are justified the same way.

"You have heard of Job's endurance, and you saw the outcome the Lord gave, for the Lord is very tender-hearted and compassionate" (James 5:11). The KJV's "the patience of Job" made Job a proverb, though the Job of the book argues with God. James praises his holding on, and points to the ending, when "the LORD turned Job's fortunes around" (Job 42:10).

Outside the Gospels the word Gehenna appears only in James 3:6: the tongue "sets fire to the wheel of existence, and Gehenna sets it on fire". The source of destructive speech is the place of final judgment itself, as Jesus warned that an insult makes a person "liable to the fire of Gehenna" (Matthew 5:22).

"More than anything, my brothers, do not take oaths, whether by heaven or by earth or with any other oath. Let your 'Yes' mean yes and your 'No' mean no" (James 5:12). The words are very close to Jesus' in Matthew 5:34-37. Whether they forbid all oaths, including in court, is discussed at Matthew 5.

James defines "clean and unspoiled religion" as visiting "orphans and widows in their trouble" and keeping oneself free of the world's stains (James 1:27), in line with the law's care for the widow and the orphan (Deuteronomy 10:18; Isaiah 1:17).

James argues from creation: we bless God with the tongue, "and we use it to curse human beings, who came into being after God's likeness" (James 3:9). As Genesis 9:6 forbids murder because humans bear God's image, James forbids cursing for the same reason.

sections.h: James and the Sermon on the Mount
sections.b: James echoes the Sermon on the Mount more than any other New Testament letter: joy in persecution (James 1:2), asking and receiving (James 1:5), doers of the word (James 1:22), the poor and the kingdom (James 2:5), mercy (James 2:13), fruit (James 3:12), peacemakers (James 3:18), two masters (James 4:4), judging (James 4:11), moth and rust (James 5:2), and oaths (James 5:12). He does not quote; he speaks the teaching in his own voice.

sections.h: The twelve tribes in the Dispersion (James 1:1)
sections.b: James writes "to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion", the Jewish name for the people of Israel scattered outside the land. Whether he means Jewish believers abroad or the whole church as a renewed Israel in exile is debated; 1 Peter 1:1 uses the same language.

sections.h: "The Judge stands right outside the doors" (James 5)
sections.b: James grounds patience in the Lord's coming (parousia): "hold out patiently until the coming of the Lord" like a farmer waiting for the rains, "because the coming of the Lord has drawn close" and "the Judge stands right outside the doors" (James 5:7-9).

Eusebius (about AD 325) wrote that the letter of James "is disputed; at least, not many of the ancients have mentioned it", though it was read publicly in very many churches, and he listed it among the disputed writings. Luther, in 1522, would not count it among "the true chief books" of the New Testament, though he did not forbid others to value it. The Council of Trent (1546) and the Westminster Confession (1646) list it among the canonical books, and every church today includes it.

"It was his will to bring us to birth by the word of truth, so that we would be a kind of firstfruits among the things he made" (James 1:18): believers are God's first share of a creation he means to renew.

sections.h: Born by the word of truth (James 1:18)
sections.b: "It was his will to bring us to birth by the word of truth" (James 1:18), set against the birth of sin from desire (James 1:15). The "word that has been rooted in you" (James 1:21) is the same word, which must be done (James 1:22).

James traces temptation not to God but to "his own desire", which conceives and gives birth to sin, and sin to death (James 1:13-15). Many readers compare the Jewish teaching of the evil inclination (yetzer hara), drawn from Genesis 8:21.

James quotes the Shema's confession and grants that it is good, but says that belief alone does not save: "The demons believe it as well, and they shiver with fear" (James 2:19). The double-minded person (James 1:8; 4:8) is the opposite of the undivided love the Shema asks for.

"The judgment will have no mercy for the one who showed none. Mercy boasts over judgment" (James 2:13). The wisdom from above is "full of mercy" (James 3:17), and the Lord is "very tender-hearted and compassionate" (James 5:11).

James uses the same Greek family for "trial" and "tempt" (James 1:2, 12-14): God tests faith so that it grows, but tempts no one to evil. "Stand up against the devil, and he will run away from you" (James 4:7).

The sick are to call "the elders of the church" to pray and anoint them (James 5:14). Whether these elders are the later order of priests (Council of Trent, session 14, canon 4) or the ordinary elders of a congregation (Calvin) is part of the dispute over the anointing of the sick.

sections.h: Confess to one another; bring back the wanderer (James 5)
sections.b: James asks believers to "confess your sins to each other and pray for each other" (James 5:16) and to turn back anyone who strays from the truth (James 5:19-20). Calvin read the first as mutual confession, not confession to a priest (Institutes 3.4.6).

In James, forgiveness comes with the prayer over the sick ("if he has done sins, they will be forgiven him", James 5:15) and with bringing back a wanderer, which "will lay a cover over a great number of sins" (James 5:20), a saying drawn from Proverbs 10:12 and shared with 1 Peter 4:8.
James calls worldly believers "adulteresses", the prophets' picture of God's people as an unfaithful wife (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 3:20): friendship with the world is unfaithfulness to God.

sections.h: Blessing and cursing from one mouth (James 3)
sections.b: "We use it to bless the Lord and Father, and we use it to curse human beings" (James 3:9). For James, the mouth that blesses God in prayer must not curse those who bear his likeness.

James sets two kinds of wisdom side by side: one earthly, natural and demonic, producing jealousy and chaos; one from above, producing peace and mercy (James 3:13-18), in the pattern of the Bible's two ways.
"Yet the grace he gives is greater. So it says, 'God takes his stand against the proud, but to the humble he gives grace'" (James 4:6), quoting the Greek of Proverbs 3:34, as 1 Peter 5:5 does.

James' word for favoritism (prosopolempsia, "receiving the face") comes from the law's command to judge without regard to rank (Leviticus 19:15). A church that seats the rich and shames the poor has become "judges whose reasoning is wicked" (James 2:4).

James asks believers to wait for the Lord's coming like a farmer for "the land's precious crop" and "the early and the late rains" (James 5:7), and says righteousness is a fruit sown in peace (James 3:18).

claude.title: Claude's theory: a letter built on Leviticus 19
claude.body: The commands of Leviticus 19:12-18 appear across James: no false oaths (James 5:12), prompt wages (James 5:4), no favoritism (James 2:1-9), no slander (James 4:11), correcting a neighbor (James 5:19-20), and the love command, which James calls the royal law (James 2:8). James may have read Leviticus 19 as the royal law spelled out. This is my own suggestion.
